Every neural network in this course finished behind a 46-coefficient LASSO, which scored 744. We
re-ran four of the five with different training and more information, and most of the gap closed.
We did not re-run Lab 8's 1D CNN, which scored 1,032.

- Shuffling the training batches improved all four networks, by 22 to 184. Every lab fed its
  network the training windows one series at a time. Shuffling them is safe once the data is split
  by time.
- Training length mattered most for the LSTM, which went from 975 at 30 epochs to 813 at the length
  a validation block chose.
- Extra features helped little. Next week's price and SNAP days can be inferred almost fully from
  the window the networks read.
- The best network ties the LASSO. An RNN with all the extra features scored 743 against the
  LASSO's 744, and no network clearly beats it.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

choice = pd.read_csv("output/validation_choice.csv")
labs = {"ffn": 1084, "rnn": 805, "lstm": 998, "transformer": 990}   # Lab 7 (5 seeds), Labs 9 Parts 1 and 2
names = {"ffn": "Feedforward", "rnn": "RNN", "lstm": "LSTM", "transformer": "Transformer"}
CRIMSON, BLUE, GRAY = "#D71920", "#005CA9", "#8A8385"

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for y, m in enumerate(["transformer", "lstm", "rnn", "ffn"]):
    retrained = choice[(choice.model == m) & (choice.features == "A")].test_mean.item()
    featured = choice[(choice.model == m) & choice.chosen_on_validation].test_mean.item()
    xs = [labs[m], retrained, featured]
    ax.plot([min(xs), max(xs)], [y, y], color=GRAY, lw=2, zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(labs[m], y, s=70, facecolor="white", edgecolor=GRAY, lw=2, zorder=3,
               label="Labs' result" if y == 0 else None)
    ax.scatter(retrained, y, s=70, color=CRIMSON, zorder=3,
               label="Same inputs, retrained" if y == 0 else None)
    ax.scatter(featured, y, s=70, color=BLUE, marker="D", zorder=4,
               label="Extra features, chosen on validation" if y == 0 else None)
ax.axvline(744, color="#1A1A1A", ls="--", lw=1)
ax.text(746, 3.45, "LASSO 744", fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.set_yticks(range(4), [names[m] for m in ["transformer", "lstm", "rnn", "ffn"]])
ax.set_xlim(700, 1100); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 3.8)
ax.set_xlabel("test RMSE, weekly units (lower is better)")
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#E6E1E2"); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

*Each filled marker is the mean of three training runs with different random seeds. Hollow markers
are the labs' recorded results. "Retrained" means shuffled training batches and a training length
chosen on a validation block. Seasonal naive, the benchmark, sits far off the right edge at 2,152.*

# The question

The course scoreboard ranks every method on the same 30 weekly sales series and the same 53 test
weeks. A LASSO with 46 hand-built features scored 744. The best neural network, a plain RNN,
scored 805. The Transformer scored 990, the LSTM 998, and the CNN 1,032.

That gap could mean the networks are the wrong tool for this data. It could also mean we trained
them badly or gave them less to work with. The LASSO knew which store and category it was
forecasting, and it knew the forecast week's own SNAP days, events, and price. The networks knew
neither.

# What stayed the same

- The data are the M5 weekly panel: 30 series (10 stores × 3 categories), units sold per week.
- We train on the weeks before May 17, 2015, and test on the 53 weeks after it, 1,590 forecasts in
  all. This is the same test block as Homework 4's LASSO.
- The models are the exact networks from the labs: Lab 7's feedforward network (26-week window),
  Lab 9 Part 1's RNN and LSTM, and Lab 9 Part 2's Transformer (52-week windows), all with the
  labs' sizes and optimizer settings.
- Every result is the mean of three runs with seeds 1, 2, and 3, reported as mean ± standard
  deviation.

# Step 1: reproduce the labs first

Before changing anything, we re-ran each lab's model exactly as the lab does. If those numbers had
not matched, any later comparison would mean nothing.

| Model | Lab's recorded result | Our re-run |
|---|---|---|
| Feedforward, 60 epochs | 1,109 · 1,176 · 946 | 1,109 · 1,176 · 946 |
| RNN, 30 epochs | 805 (seeds 1–2) | 805 |
| LSTM, 30 epochs | 998 (seeds 1–2) | 998 |
| Transformer, 30 epochs | 1,013 · 967 | 1,013 · 967 |

All four matched. Every difference below comes from what we changed, not from a different setup.

# Step 2: change one thing at a time

## Training order

A PyTorch `DataLoader` with `shuffle=False` serves the training windows in the order they were
built, series by series. Each batch then comes from a single store and category, and the model
spends a stretch of every pass on one series before moving to the next. With `shuffle=True`,
every batch mixes all 30 series.

Shuffling the training windows does not leak the future. Every training window still ends before
the test period, and each window carries its own past. What leaks is shuffling or splitting at
random *before* the time split. The labs used `shuffle=False` so that a run repeats exactly. A
shuffled run with a fixed seed repeats exactly too: we ran the same shuffled RNN twice and got
752.591 both times. The number of CPU threads can change a result slightly, so two of our
Transformer runs with the same seed and different thread settings scored 859 and 862.

## Training length, chosen honestly

The labs trained for a fixed 30 or 60 epochs. Picking a longer length because it scored best on
the test weeks would quietly use the test set to tune the model. Instead we followed Lecture 7's
advice on early stopping and let a validation block decide:

1. Set aside the last 52 weeks of the training period as a validation block.
2. Train on the weeks before it, and note the epoch with the lowest validation error.
3. Retrain on the whole training period for that many epochs, then score the test weeks once.

## Features

We gave each network the information the LASSO had, in groups:

- Which series: store and category as one-hot columns.
- The forecast week itself: its SNAP days, event days, price, and week of the year. These join the
  network's final layer, or its inputs for the feedforward network.
- All of the above, plus the week of the year for every week in the window.

Which feature set counts for each network was also chosen on the validation block, never on the
test weeks.

# Results

## Training order, at the labs' own training lengths

| Model | Lab order | Shuffled | Change |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Feedforward (60 epochs) | 1,077 ± 96 | 893 ± 60 | −184 |
| RNN (30 epochs) | 820 ± 21 | 752 ± 1 | −68 |
| LSTM (30 epochs) | 997 ± 2 | 975 ± 0 | −22 |
| Transformer (30 epochs) | 950 ± 60 | 859 ± 30 | −91 |

*The lab-order rows here use three seeds, so the RNN shows 820 rather than the scoreboard's
two-seed 805.*

## Training length, shuffled, the labs' inputs

| Model | 30 epochs | 60 | 100 | Chosen on validation | Epochs chosen |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| Feedforward | 850 | 893 | 890 | 877 ± 43 | 30–51 |
| RNN | 752 | 752 | 779 | 779 ± 2 | 62–97 |
| LSTM | 975 | 845 | 773 | 813 ± 14 | 139–148 of 150 |
| Transformer | 859 | 840 | 842 | 840 ± 22 | 43–98 |

## Features, shuffled, training length chosen on validation

| Model | Labs' inputs | + series | + forecast week | All | Chosen on validation |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Feedforward | 877 | 972 | 839 | 926 | 926 (all) |
| RNN | 779 | 789 | 781 | 743 | **743 (all)** |
| LSTM | 813 | 783 | 821 | 820 | 783 (+ series) |
| Transformer | 840 | · | · | 817 | 817 (all) |
| *LASSO, 46 features* | | | | | *744* |
| *XGBoost* | | | | | *781 (792 with the course's pinned version)* |
| *Seasonal naive* | | | | | *2,152* |

*For the Transformer we ran only the labs' inputs and the full feature set under validation,
because each run takes several minutes.*

# Why it came out this way

## Unshuffled batches make the model less stable

With `shuffle=False`, each batch comes from one series, so each update follows that series' error
rather than the panel's. We watched the last training pass batch by batch, scoring the test weeks
after every update, to see what that does.

| Model | Test RMSE range across the last pass, lab order | Shuffled | Series better just after their own stretch, lab order | Shuffled |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|
| Feedforward | 841–1,665 | · | 19 of 30 | · |
| RNN | 784–909 | 736–828 | 17 | 15 |
| LSTM | 974–1,137 | · | 15 | · |
| Transformer | 884–1,235 | 816–955 | 16 | 14 |

*Means of three seeds. A dot means we did not run that case. The last two columns count the series
whose test error, right after the batch that ends that series' stretch of the pass, is below its
median for the pass. Chance is 15, and in a shuffled run there is no real stretch, so those runs
are the control.*

The first two columns show the instability. Under the lab order, the test score swings widely within
a single pass, so a final score depends partly on which batch training happens to stop on. In the two
models where we ran the control, shuffling narrowed the swing and lowered it.

The last two columns test a natural explanation, that the model ends each pass tuned toward the
series it saw last. The data give that little support: a series is barely more likely to be
well fit right after its own stretch than a shuffled run would suggest. We can say what shuffling
changes, but these measurements do not show exactly why it helps.

## Series identity under the labs' order

The store and category columns made the lab-order Transformer far worse, 950 to 1,850. The training
error rose too, so this was not overfitting. The week-to-week error did not change, and all of the
damage was in each series' overall level. Once the batches were shuffled, the same columns were
harmless (853).

Each series' identity weights move mostly during its own stretch of each pass, so we checked whether
they fall out of step with the rest of the model afterward. Partly, they do. Measured on the training
windows, the typical level error was about 970 right after a series' own stretch and about 1,410 by
the end of the pass, against 190 and 260 when shuffled. The error grows after a series' stretch, in
all three seeds, but most of it is already there before that growth begins, so falling out of step is
at most part of the story.

## The LSTM was undertrained

At 30 epochs the shuffled LSTM scored 975, well behind the RNN's 752. At 100 epochs it scored 773,
ahead of the RNN's 779. Lecture 9 Part 1 warned that a comparison can flip with the training budget,
and these two models flipped.

With the labs' inputs, validation chose 139 to 148 epochs for the LSTM, which scored 813. That is worse than the
773 from a fixed 100 epochs, so more epochs were not simply better on the test weeks. We report 813
as the honest figure, because choosing 100 after seeing the test weeks would use the test set to
tune the model.

## Next week's price and SNAP days could be inferred from the window

A network reads the weeks before the forecast week, 52 for the sequence models and 26 for the
feedforward network, so it never sees the forecast week's own values. But two of the three are almost
fully predictable from a 52-week window:

| Forecast week's… | Share predictable from the window | Why |
|---|--:|---|
| Price | 99% | Next week's average price is almost always within 1% of last week's. |
| SNAP days | 91% | SNAP follows a fixed monthly calendar, and the window starts one year back. |
| Event days | 13% | Holidays move. This is new information, but events barely move weekly sales. |

So the forecast-week features gave the networks either something they could already infer or
something that matters little at the weekly level.

## Validation is a guide, not an oracle

For the feedforward network, the validation block preferred the full feature set (926 on the test
weeks), while the forecast-week features alone would have scored 839. The validation year and the
test year differ. Choosing on validation is still right, because picking 839 after seeing that it
won on the test weeks would make the number meaningless.

# What this changes, and what it does not

The scoreboard numbers were measured correctly. Each one is what that lab's setup produces, and we
reproduced every one. What changes is the lesson drawn from them. The four networks we re-ran
trailed the LASSO largely because of how they were trained. With shuffled batches, a validated
training length, and the extra features, the best network ties a 46-coefficient linear model, and
none beats it clearly. On 30 series with about 5,000 training
windows, a well-built linear model is still as good as anything in the course, and it is far
simpler to explain.

::: {.callout-tip}
## For your homework and final project

- Split by time first. After that, shuffle the training batches, with a fixed seed. Homework 5 is
  the exception: it specifies `shuffle=False`, so follow the assignment there.
- Choose training length, and any other setting, on a validation block taken from the training
  period. Never choose on the test weeks.
- Run more than one seed, and report the mean and the spread.
- Reproduce the original result before changing anything, so you know your changes caused the
  difference.
- Before adding a feature, ask whether the model can already infer it from what it sees.
- When a result looks wrong, compare training error with test error, and level error with
  week-to-week error. That tells you which kind of failure you have.
:::

# Limits

- All results come from one test block of 53 weeks. A different year could rank the models
  differently.
- Each result uses three seeds. Spreads in the tables above run from near zero to about 100, so
  differences of a few dozen are within the noise.
- We varied only training order, training length, and features. Network size, learning rate, and
  dropout stayed at the labs' values, and the LASSO was not re-tuned.
- Lab 8's CNN was not re-run, so we cannot say how much of its gap comes from the setup.
- Validation's epoch choices for the LSTM sat near the 150-epoch limit we set, and one seed reached
  it, so a higher limit could change what validation picks.

# Rerun it yourself

The code is in the course repository under `explorations/transformer-features/`. From the
repository root, with the course environment active:

```bash
python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/run_features.py            # labs' order, 30 epochs
SHUFFLE=1 python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/run_features.py  # shuffled batches
SHUFFLE=1 EPOCHS=100 MODEL=rnn python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/run_features.py A B C D
VALID=1 SHUFFLE=1 EPOCHS=150 MODEL=lstm python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/run_features.py A
MODEL=ffn WINDOW=26 EPOCHS=100 python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/run_features.py A
MODEL=transformer python explorations/transformer-features/scripts/test_mechanism.py A B   # the last pass, batch by batch
```

`MODEL` is `transformer` (default), `rnn`, `lstm`, or `ffn`. The letters choose feature sets: A is
the labs' inputs, B adds the series, C adds the forecast week, D adds everything.
`scripts/summarize.py` rebuilds the full results table, `output/validation_choice.csv` records which
feature set the validation block chose for each network, and `output/mechanism.csv` holds the
batch-by-batch measurements.
